title: Functions: multiple returns, named results, variadic, closures
summary: Go functions return several values, and (value, error) is the idiom every API follows. Variadic parameters are slices, and closures capture variables, not copies.

examples.title: (value, error), named results and the min/max builtins

annotations.note: The error is a second return value, so the caller can't use the result without at least seeing it. On failure, return the zero value plus the error.
Named results document what comes back and start at their zero value. A naked return returns them as they are, handy here, confusing in long functions. min and max are builtins since Go 1.21.
q and err exist only inside each if. errors.Is compares against the ErrDivByZero sentinel, which keeps working when someone wraps the error.
The standard library uses the same (value, error) shape everywhere, so callers handle every failure the same way.

examples.title: Variadic parameters are slices; closures keep state

annotations.note: Inside the function nums is a plain []int. sum() with no arguments gets a nil slice, which ranges zero times.
xs... passes the slice itself, not a copy, so double writes into the caller's backing array. Callers who don't expect that get a surprise.
The closure captures the variable count, not its value at creation. Each call to counter makes a new count, so counters don't share state.
Arguments are evaluated left to right, so the output is 1 2 3 1: the second counter starts fresh.
Functions are values: assign them, pass them, return them. A function type like func(string) string is often all the interface you need.

use_cases: (T, error) results for anything that can fail: parsing, I/O, lookups
Named results when a deferred function must adjust them (see the defer lesson)
Variadic helpers: fmt.Println, append, slices.Concat, option lists
Closures for counters, memoization, and callbacks passed to sort or http handlers
strengths: Errors are visible in every signature; unlike Java's unchecked exceptions, a call that can fail looks different from one that can't
Multiple returns remove out-parameters (C) and throwaway tuple or result classes (Java)
Closures are lightweight and capture by reference, like JS closures, with no 'effectively final' rule as in Java lambdas
weaknesses: No default parameters and no overloading: options become structs, variadic option functions, or several functions with different names
if err != nil repeats in every caller; there is no ? operator as in Rust
Variadic calls with slice... share the caller's backing array, an aliasing rule that is easy to forget

pitfalls.title: Ignoring the error with _
pitfalls.detail: v, _ := f() compiles and silently drops failures. Reserve _ for errors that genuinely can't happen, and say why in a comment.

pitfalls.title: Naked returns in long functions
pitfalls.detail: A bare return far from the result declarations hides what is returned. Keep naked returns for short functions.

pitfalls.title: Expecting xs... to copy
pitfalls.detail: The callee receives the caller's slice; writes are visible to the caller. Copy with slices.Clone when that's not wanted.

quiz.q: Inside func f(nums ...int), what is the type of nums?
quiz.why: A variadic parameter is an ordinary slice inside the function.

quiz.q: c1, c2 := counter(), counter(); fmt.Println(c1(), c1(), c2()). What prints?
quiz.why: Each counter() call creates its own captured count variable.

quiz.q: What should a function return together with a non-nil error?
options: The zero value of the result type, unless the docs say otherwise
quiz.why: Callers must not use the result when err != nil; returning the zero value makes accidental use harmless.

further_reading.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Function types
The Go Programming Language Specification: Min and max

body:
## Concept

A Go function can return several values. The convention for anything that can fail is
`(result, error)` with the error last; callers check it before touching the result. Results
can be named, which documents them and lets a `defer` change them. A final parameter
`...T` accepts any number of `T` and arrives as a `[]T`. Functions are first-class
values, and function literals are closures over the variables they mention.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C: multiple returns replace out-parameters and `errno`.
- Java: no checked or unchecked exceptions for ordinary failures; the error is part of the
  return type. No overloading and no default arguments.
- Python: multiple returns look like tuple returns, but they aren't a tuple value; you
  can't store `f()` in one variable when f returns two results.
- JS/TS: closures work the same way (capture by reference). Rest parameters `...xs`
  correspond to variadic `...T`.

## Design notes

Return errors, don't print them: the caller knows whether a failure matters. Keep
signatures small; when you need optional parameters, take an options struct rather than
inventing overloads. Name results when they clarify (`(lo, hi int)`) or when a deferred
function must touch them, and otherwise leave them unnamed. When a function only needs
one behavior from its caller, accept a function value instead of an interface.
